options.explanation: OIL stands for exactly that half of the electron picture.
Losing oxygen is reduction, not oxidation.
Heat is not part of the definition.
Protons never transfer in redox definitions.

questions.stem: Which change is reduction under the oxygen-transfer definition?

options.explanation: That is reduction, but under the electron lens, not the oxygen one.
Removing oxygen is the reductive half of that lens.
Gaining oxygen is oxidation.
Losing hydrogen is oxidation under the hydrogen lens.

questions.stem: A metal atom becomes a metal ion. Under which definition has it been oxidised?

options.explanation: No oxygen is required for the ionisation itself.
Losing electrons is oxidation by definition.

options.text: Electron transfer - it has lost electrons
options.explanation: Ion formation strips electrons, the oxidation side of OIL RIG.
No hydrogen participates when a bare metal ionises.

questions.stem: Why do the three definitions never contradict each other?

options.explanation: The definitions apply to any redox species alike.

options.text: Only the electron definition is correct
options.explanation: All three are valid descriptive layers.

options.text: They apply in different branches with different outcomes
options.explanation: The outcomes always match; the branch only chooses the lens.

options.text: They describe the same charge shift through three different transfers
options.explanation: Oxygen, hydrogen and electron transfers all move charge, so all three lenses agree.

questions.stem: When sodium meets chlorine, which species has lost electrons?

options.text: Sodium, which loses its outer electron to chlorine
options.explanation: Electron loss is oxidation.
Chlorine gains the electron and is reduced.
A transfer clearly occurs.
One species must be reduced to accept the electrons.

questions.stem: State what OIL RIG stands for.
questions.modelAnswer: OIL RIG means Oxidation Is Loss and Reduction Is Gain, referring to electrons in every redox reaction.

questions.stem: List the three definitions of oxidation.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation is gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, or loss of electrons.

questions.stem: Explain why gaining oxygen and losing electrons describe the same outcome in a metal-plus-oxygen reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen atoms accept electrons when they bond, so a metal that adds oxygen is simultaneously surrendering electrons to it - the oxygen lens and the electron lens film one transfer.

questions.stem: A 2.0 g magnesium sample loses 0.16 g worth of electron mass equivalents when it oxidises - expressed properly, each Mg atom loses 2 electrons. How many electrons does one Mg atom lose, and is it oxidised or reduced?
questions.modelAnswer: One magnesium atom loses 2 electrons and is therefore oxidised under the electron definition.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of Fe in the simple ion Fe3+?

options.explanation: That would be the Fe2+ case.
The charge on a simple ion is its oxidation number.
The sign follows the ion, which is positive.
Zero belongs to free elements, not ions.

questions.stem: What oxidation number does a free, uncombined element carry?

options.explanation: Negative values need bonding partners.
The rule is uniform: zero for all free elements.
Uncombined elements such as He or C read zero.
No charge exists to assign.

questions.stem: Which oxidation number does oxygen carry in almost all compounds?

options.explanation: Oxygen is rarely positive; that is a fluoride exception class.
Zero applies only to free O2.
-1 belongs to peroxides, the exception class.
The -2 default stands unless peroxides or fluorides override it.

questions.stem: Why does the rule table fix Group 1 metals at +1?

options.text: Each Group 1 atom has one outer electron it always loses in compounds
options.explanation: Surrendering one electron leaves a fixed +1 state.
The number of protons varies down the group.
They react readily, forming fixed +1 ions.

options.text: Oxygen forces that value on them
options.explanation: Oxygen's own rule comes later in the hierarchy.

questions.stem: A compound contains only sodium and oxygen. What is the oxidation number of sodium?

options.explanation: No such sodium state exists.
Group 1 metals are +1 in compounds regardless of partner.
That is the Group 2 tag.
Metals never carry negative states here.

questions.stem: State the oxidation numbers of Fe2+, O2- and Al3+.
questions.modelAnswer: Fe2+ carries +2, O2- carries -2, and Al3+ carries +3 - each equals its ion charge.

questions.stem: Recite the first four rules of the oxidation-number table.
questions.modelAnswer: Free elements are zero; Group 1 metals are +1 and Group 2 metals are +2 in compounds; fluorine is always -1; oxygen is normally -2.

questions.stem: Explain why the oxidation number of a simple ion equals its charge.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxidation number is defined as the charge the atom would carry if bonding were completely ionic; for an ion that bonding already is ionic, so by definition the notional charge and the real charge coincide.

questions.stem: A sample contains Fe2+ and Fe3+ in a 3-to-1 ratio. If the average iron ion carries charge x, compute x.
questions.modelAnswer: Three ions at +2 plus one at +3 give 9 charge units over 4 ions, so the average is +2.25.

questions.stem: In CO2, which element carries the negative oxidation number and why?

options.explanation: A neutral compound cannot sum positive-only to zero.
Same objection - the sum must reach zero.

options.text: Oxygen, because it is more electronegative than carbon
options.explanation: Electronegativity ordering fixes the sign.

options.text: Carbon, because it is written first
options.explanation: Formula order carries no sign information.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of carbon in CO2?

options.explanation: Carbon is the less electronegative partner.
That value belongs to carbon in CO.
Carbon is bonded here, not free.
Two oxygens at -2 force carbon to +4 for the zero sum.

questions.stem: Which Stock name fits the variable oxidation state in Fe2O3?

options.explanation: Two irons at +3 balance three oxygens at -2.
That name belongs to FeO.
Stock notation avoids the prefix when the state is stated.
That is the prefix name, not the Stock name.

questions.stem: What oxidation number does manganese carry in the manganate(VII) ion, MnO4-?

options.explanation: That value belongs to potassium, outside the ion.
Four oxygens give -8; the ion's -1 charge forces Mn to +7.
That would leave the sum at -2, breaking the ion charge.
No such manganese state appears in this ion.

questions.stem: Why are Roman numerals unnecessary in 'sulfur dioxide'?

options.explanation: The prefix counts atoms, not oxidation states.

options.text: Sulfur's state is zero in that compound
options.explanation: Bonded sulfur is not zero.

options.text: Sulfur shows only one common positive state with oxygen, so no ambiguity exists
options.explanation: Stock notation earns its keep only for variable states.

options.text: Non-metals never receive Roman numerals by law
options.explanation: The convention simply sees less use where no ambiguity exists.

questions.stem: State the rule governing the sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound.
questions.modelAnswer: In a neutral molecule or compound, the oxidation numbers of all the atoms add up to exactly zero.

questions.stem: Write the Stock names of FeO and Fe2O3.
questions.modelAnswer: FeO is iron(II) oxide and Fe2O3 is iron(III) oxide - the Roman numeral reports the metal's state.

questions.stem: Explain how electronegativity decides which element in a binary compound takes the negative oxidation number.
questions.modelAnswer: The more electronegative element attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so in the fully ionic picture it owns them and reads negative, leaving the other element positive.

questions.stem: Sulfur shows +4 in one oxide and +6 in another. Write both Stock-style formulas with oxygen at -2 and verify each sums to zero.
questions.modelAnswer: SO2: +4 plus 2(-2) sums to 0; SO3: +6 plus 3(-2) sums to 0 - both neutral compounds check out.

questions.stem: What oxidation number does hydrogen carry in sodium hydride, NaH?

options.explanation: That is hydrogen's usual state in covalent compounds, not in hydrides.
Bonded hydrogen is never zero here.
No such hydrogen state exists.
Sodium's +1 forces hydrogen to -1 in the neutral compound.

questions.stem: What oxidation number does each oxygen carry in hydrogen peroxide, H2O2?

options.explanation: Two hydrogens at +1 force each oxygen to -1.

Bonded oxygen is not free.

options.explanation: No doubling exists in the convention.
Nitrate's atoms sum to -1, sulfate's to -2, and so on.

options.explanation: The six oxygens carry -2 each, totalling -12.
Tetrathionate carries a 2- charge.

options.text: Four sulfur atoms sit in two different environments sharing a total of +10

questions.stem: Which chain correctly sums oxidation numbers inside the nitrite ion, NO2-?

options.explanation: Each oxygen is -2, not -1.
The electronegative partner is negative.

options.text: The ion is neutral so nitrogen is zero
options.explanation: The ion carries -1.

options.text: Two oxygens give -4; the ion charge is -1; so nitrogen is +3

questions.stem: State the oxidation number of hydrogen in metal hydrides and of oxygen in peroxides.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen carries -1 in metal hydrides and oxygen carries -1 in peroxides.

questions.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of nitrogen in the nitrate ion, NO3-.
questions.modelAnswer: Three oxygens give -6 and the ion charge is -1, so nitrogen carries +5.

questions.stem: Explain why hydrogen must be -1 in NaH using the zero-sum rule.
questions.modelAnswer: NaH is neutral and sodium, as a Group 1 metal, is +1; the zero sum forces hydrogen to -1, which also matches its hydride-ion identity.

questions.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of chlorine in the chlorate(V) ion, ClO3-, showing the ion-sum equation.
questions.modelAnswer: x + 3(-2) = -1 gives x = +5, so chlorine carries +5 in the chlorate(V) ion.
